Protect corridors and sites

Right-of-way and servitude monitoring from the air

Know what stands inside your right of way, how close each structure is to the line, and what has changed since the last survey. We start with a dated baseline register, re-survey on a schedule agreed with you, and send a notice after each survey saying what changed and where. A person reviews every result before it reaches you.

Used in: Oil & gas · Power & utilities · Rail & roads

Request a proposal See a reviewed sample

What it is

A dated register of what stands inside your right of way

A right of way, servitude, wayleave or protection zone only protects a line while it stays clear. Encroachment rarely arrives all at once. A cooking shelter goes up beside a field, then a house, a fence line and a track to reach it. Between patrols and helicopter flights nobody sees it happen, and by the time it is noticed the structure is a compensation question, a safety concern and, later, a dispute about who was there first.

Right-of-way monitoring replaces that uncertainty with a record. We map the structures within the distances that apply to your line, measure each one to the route you supply, and rate every 500 m of route for encroachment density, so your land and integrity teams know which stretches to visit first. Then we repeat the survey on an agreed schedule and tell you what changed.

The method is the same whatever your industry calls the strip: a pipeline right of way, a Mozambican zona de protecção parcial, a South African servitude or a Nigerian power-line right of way. What stands within X metres of the line, and since when?

Encroachment density, not risk

Each 500 m segment is rated High (more than 5 structures inside the widest buffer), Medium (1 to 5) or Low (none). It is a count rule that helps you prioritise. It is not a safety, hazard or integrity assessment. See the methodology.

Statutory widths

The strips we measure against, country by country

We report the distances you choose. These are the widths set in law for the lines we survey most often, as of 26 September 2026. This section summarises public rules for information. It is not legal advice; the sources are linked.

Zona de protecção parcial

Mozambique

  • Lei n.º 19/97, de 1 de Outubro (Lei de Terras), arts. 8 and 9: a partial protection zone of 50 m on each side of oil, gas, water, electricity and telecommunications lines, where no land-use right (DUAT) can be acquired, only special licences. Railways: 50 m each side of the axis. Roads: 30 m (primary) and 15 m (secondary and tertiary).
  • Lei n.º 8/2026, de 3 de Junho (Petroleum Law), art. 75: a 50 m partial protection zone around petroleum infrastructure; the safety zone is set by regulation.
  • Lei n.º 12/2022, de 11 de Julho (Electricity Law), art. 43: an administrative servitude of up to 50 m from the line’s axis, registered against the concession. Compensation is not owed to holders who acquired their rights after the line was built (art. 43(10)).

Servitudes and road reserves

South Africa

  • The registered servitude: pipeline, power-line and bulk-water widths are set in each servitude agreement and diagram.
  • SANRAL Act 7 of 1998, s48: on national roads, structures in the building restriction area (outside urban areas, within 60 m of the road boundary) need SANRAL’s written permission.

Rights of way

Nigeria

  • Oil Pipelines Act, s.12: on the licence holder’s application, buildings and cultivation can be restricted within a specified distance, of up to 100 feet, from the land in the pipeline licence.
  • NESIS Regulations 2015, Table 3.1: power-line rights of way of 50 m (330 kV), 30 m (132 kV) and 11 m (33 kV and 11 kV), divided equally either side of the centre line, with no structures under the line.

Two of these rules show why the date of a record matters. Mozambique’s Electricity Law ties compensation to whether rights were acquired before or after the line was built, and NESIS limits a licensee’s liability for structures built after the line. A dated register supports those processes: it records what stood where on the imagery date. It does not decide them.

How it works

Baseline first, then scheduled re-surveys

  1. Route and widths

    You send the route as KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage, or we draw it with you and you confirm it. We agree the distances: the statutory strip, your company standard, and a wider band to watch.

  2. Baseline register

    We map the structures along the whole line from dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or imagery you already hold. A reviewer confirms, removes and adds structures by hand, and anything the imagery cannot settle goes to a “verify on the ground” list.

  3. Scheduled re-surveys

    On the cadence we agree, we survey the line again on new dated imagery. New and removed structures are flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views of each change.

  4. Change notice and close checks

    After each survey your team receives a notice of what changed and where. Where a flagged stretch needs more detail, a drone survey captures it, subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires.

Alongside the register, a survey can add the signals that tend to come before new structures: new tracks and fresh digging on or near the right of way, how built-up land around the line has grown year by year, and notices of satellite-detected fire hotspots near above-ground installations.

What you receive

Files your land, integrity and GIS teams can use straight away

  • A structure register: each structure’s ID, distance to the line, buffer band, chainage and coordinates in WGS84 and UTM, and a photo crop
  • An encroachment-density table for every 500 m of route
  • Change layers after each re-survey: new, removed and unchanged structures, with before-and-after views
  • A change notice by email to the contacts you name
  • A PDF report in English or Portuguese, with maps, route tables and the register
  • GIS layers in GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile, and an interactive map file that opens in a browser, including in the field

The services behind it

Every proposal names the services it includes. These are the ones this solution draws on.

Encroachment and structure mapping

  • Right-of-way encroachment surveyA register of the structures within the distances you choose from your pipeline, power line, road or railway. Each structure comes with its distance to the line and its coordinates, and each stretch of the route gets an encroachment-density rating.

Change and repeat surveys

  • Change detection between dated surveysNew and removed structures between two or more dated surveys, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views of each change.
  • Scheduled re-surveys with change noticesYour route or site re-surveyed on a schedule agreed with you, with an email to your team after each survey saying what has changed and where.
  • Settlement growth trendsHow built-up land has changed year by year around your assets, showing where settlement pressure is growing.
  • Fire hotspot and burn-scar watchNotices of satellite-detected fire hotspots near your lines, pipelines, plantations and sites, and maps of burnt areas after the fire.

Detection of specific features

  • Track and access-route mappingNew tracks and access roads into your concession, across your right of way or around your site, mapped between dates.
  • Excavation and third-party works on rights of wayFresh digging, spoil heaps, trenches and earthworks on or near your pipeline or cable right of way, flagged between surveys so your field teams know where to check.

Drone and imagery

  • Drone checks of flagged areasSatellite screening narrows the search, then drone flights over the flagged stretches capture the detail your team needs, subject to the permits each job requires.

Reports and delivery

  • Interactive map fileA self-contained interactive map of your results that your team can open in a web browser, including in the field.

Limits

What right-of-way monitoring is not

What it shows

  • The structures visible from above within the widths you set, and their distance to the line
  • What changed between two dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Which stretches carry the most structures, and where to send people first
  • Works, tracks and cleared ground visible at the surface

What it does not show

  • Anything between surveys: it is scheduled, never continuous
  • The condition of the pipe or line, leaks, taps or any integrity measure
  • Who lives in a structure, who owns it, or whether it is authorised
  • Structures hidden under dense canopy, and a cadastral or statutory survey of the strip

Who uses it

Built for the teams answerable for a line

Oil & gas

Right-of-way, land and integrity teams on gas, crude and fuel pipelines: structures in the protection zone, counts for class-location reviews, and fresh digging near the line.

Pipeline rights of way

Power & utilities

Servitude and line-maintenance teams on transmission and distribution lines and bulk-water pipelines: what has been built under or beside the line, and which stretches to engage first.

Line servitudes and wayleaves

Rail & roads

Corridor managers on railways and roads: structures in reserves and building restriction areas, new informal crossings and tracks, and change between surveys.

Road and rail reserves

Also used by project finance and ESIA teams monitoring a financed corridor, and by renewables developers along their connection lines.

Frequently asked questions

How often is the line re-surveyed?

On a schedule agreed with you, never in real time. Satellites and drones capture images on particular dates, so we re-survey your line on that schedule and send a notice after each survey. How often depends on when new imagery of your area is available, on cloud and, for drone flights, on permits. We set the cadence per project and write it into the proposal.

Which widths can you measure against?

Any that matter to you. Most clients use the statutory strip for their country and asset, plus their company standard or a lender requirement. One survey can report up to six distances, measured from the route you supply, in the route’s local UTM zone.

Does this replace our patrols or line walks?

No. It tells your patrols and field teams where to look first, and it gives you a dated record between visits. Anything the imagery cannot settle is listed for a check on the ground.

What does a change notice contain?

An email to the contacts you name, after each re-survey, saying how many structures are new or gone, where they are by chainage and stretch, and which stretches changed rating. It links to the updated report and GIS layers. Every change in it has been confirmed by a reviewer.

Do you decide whether a structure is allowed?

No. We map what stands on the land and measure it against the widths you give us. Whether a structure is authorised, and what happens next, is for you and the authorities to decide.

Send us your route and the widths that apply to it.

KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage, or we can draw the line with you. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
